items.title: Home
items.content:
Notes from a small farm: what we planted, what the soil said, and what we would do differently next year.

New posts go under Posts in the outline; the newest ten show up below, and every one of them is in the archive.

items.title: About
items.content: Written by the people who work the back forty. This is an ordinary page: edit it like any other.

items.title: Posts
items.content: Every post lives under this page. It stays out of the menu; the archive lists them all.

items.title: Planting the north beds
items.content:
The frost held off until the first week of November this year, which gave the garlic a full three weeks to root before the ground hardened.Hardneck garlic wants about four to six weeks of root growth before the soil freezes.

We split the north beds into four rows of hardneck and two of softneck, mulched with straw from the east field, and marked each row with the variety and date.

items.title: What the soil test said
items.content:
The extension office sent back the soil report in nine days. Phosphorus is high, potassium is fine, and the pH sits at 6.4, close enough to leave alone.

The surprise was organic matter: 2.1 percent, lower than the compost we have been adding would suggest.

items.title: Saving tomato seed
items.content:
Fermenting the seed for three days in a jar of its own pulp lifts off the gel coat.

Rinse, dry on a plate for a week, and label the envelope before you forget which plant they came from.

items.title: Mulch, measured
items.content:
Straw at four inches kept the beds two degrees warmer than bare ground through December.

Leaves did almost as well, but matted down by February.
